extracted.intended_audience: regulatory agencies, lawmakers, advocacy groups, vendors/lead_generators, and enforcement officials
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommended legal/technical practices to ensure integrity, authenticity, and accountability in notice-and-comment public submissions and to deter astroturfing, impersonation, and automated/fraudulent bulk filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandate disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Require that intermediaries disclose, with each comment or message submitted, the intermediary’s identity and the identities of any parties that assisted in generating or submitting the comments and messages; disclosure may be in the comment text or in viewable metadata and must be available to the public as part of the comment process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to trace fraudulent submissions, reveal involved interested parties, enable public and press oversight, and rebuild trust. Example mechanisms: text notation (e.g., “This comment was solicited and submitted by Company A, on behalf of Non-Profit X.”) or separate metadata fields/registration for mass submissions. GSA/Regulations.gov API identity-validation is a cited starting point but should be expanded to identify advocacy sponsors as well as vendors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold intermediaries to account
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should impose consequences on advocacy groups and vendors that submit fake submissions, with penalties proportional to number of fake submissions, whether conduct was intentional or inadvertent, and what preventive measures were in place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences may include suspension of submission privileges, civil fines, and other sanctions. The goal is to shift incentives so parties that run campaigns and their vendors actively detect and prevent fraud rather than prioritizing volume. Recordkeeping and monitoring of subcontractors are prerequisites for accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit deceptive and unauthorized comments (statutory rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislatures should prohibit knowingly submitting, or causing to be submitted, two or more comments or messages to the government (a) that are intended to deceive or (b) on behalf of someone else without using reasonable measures to verify authorization through express, informed consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A federal/state law would require advocacy groups to confirm valid consent and would prohibit most fake submissions including those using fictitious identities intended to deceive. The law should include meaningful penalties (substantial civil fines) and expressly authorize state attorneys general to enforce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen impersonation laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Amend criminal impersonation statutes to provide substantial penalties when many individuals are impersonated before a government agency or official, recognizing large-scale misuse differs from existing single-person impersonation provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current federal and state statutes (e.g., 18 U.S.C. § 1001; N.Y. Penal Law § 190.25) were not designed for mass impersonation; reforms should make penalties commensurate with scale and harms to deter misuse of many identities in rulemaking dockets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require express, informed consent before submitting on someone's behalf
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermediaries must secure and retain explicit, informed consent from an individual before submitting a comment or message to government on their behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlements referenced require express informed consent; consent should be specific (showing the text to be submitted or clearly notifying the submitter) and documented/stored to enable later verification and investigations. Anti-patterns include copying previously collected leads or using 'show-me' sites to fabricate proof of consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust consumer disclosures in lead-generation campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: When collecting leads or soliciting comments (e.g., via co-registration, sweepstakes, or online ads), vendors must provide clear, prominent disclosures to consumers about who is soliciting the comment, how their data will be used, and whether a comment will be submitted on their behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosures should prevent consumers from being unknowingly enrolled; examples of abusive practices include co-registration sites that mix commercial offers with hidden comment solicitations or 'show-me' sites used to deceive clients about live traffic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity validation and registration for mass/API submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Require entities seeking authorization to use agency comment submission APIs or to submit large volumes of comments to first identify and validate their identity (as GSA does for Regulations.gov) and register their role and sponsors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identity validation is a starting point; agencies should expand requirements to ensure advocacy sponsors—not just vendors—are identified and that identity information is publicly available. This helps trace source of bulk submissions and spot organized campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical safeguards against automated submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should implement technical measures—such as CAPTCHA, rate limiting, bot-detection services, and other automated-traffic mitigation techniques—to detect and block mass automated submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CAPTCHA is recommended as an initial step but insufficient alone; combine with rate limiting, anomaly detection, IP and user-behavior analytics, third-party bot-detection platforms, and logging. Agencies with budget constraints may partner with private-sector actors for technology and support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and mitigate bulk/fraudulent patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should monitor comment dockets for red flags of fraud (e.g., massive submissions from single sources, recurring identical language, fictitious e-mail domains, deceased signers, reused purchased lists, abnormal address patterns) and have procedures to audit and mitigate suspect submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the FCC docket: millions of identical comments, submissions using deceased individuals' names, internet domains indicative of fictitious accounts. Agencies should be prepared to flag, quarantine, or discount suspect comments pending verification and should publish findings where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require vendor oversight, subcontractor monitoring, and record retention
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaign organizers and advocacy groups must carefully monitor subcontractors, retain records of solicitations and consent, and maintain logs sufficient to facilitate oversight and investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlements with Fluent, React2Media, and Opt-Intelligence required monitoring and record retention. Practical measures include audit trails, timestamped screenshots of solicitations, consent records, vendor attestations, and access to underlying lead-generation data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make intermediary-identifying metadata public in dockets
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure any identifying metadata submitted with comments (e.g., vendor/intermediary names, sponsor IDs, submission method) is viewable in public dockets so press, researchers, and the public can analyze and surface abuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public metadata enables crowd-sourced detection of astroturfing and fraud. The report notes GSA’s steps for Regulations.gov as a model but urges broader disclosure requirements across agencies (including congressional email systems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve legitimate anonymous comments while protecting against fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Reforms should not foreclose anonymous comments; anonymous submissions (e.g., signed 'anonymous') should be allowed but agencies should balance privacy with fraud protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymous comments that are not intended to deceive should not be penalized; however, agencies should apply safeguards to verify the legitimacy of anonymous bulk submissions and should make clear the distinction between anonymous privacy-protecting submissions and deceptive anonymous mass filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure penalties are meaningful and enforceable (deterrence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil fines and other penalties for fraudulent or unauthorized comment submissions should be substantial enough to make fraud costly, not merely a business expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties should be scalable by harm and number of individuals impersonated; state attorneys general should be expressly authorized to bring enforcement actions where resident data were misused. Settlements cited included multimillion-dollar payments and injunctive reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require disclosure of advocacy groups’ role in campaign solicitations and dockets
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocacy groups that sponsor or run campaigns must be identified both to the government and publicly in any comment docket; clients' and sponsors' roles should not be concealed behind ostensibly independent non-profits or vendors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report highlights astroturfing practices where industry funding was hidden by recruiting unrelated advocacy groups; remedy requires transparent branding and sponsor disclosure on solicitations and in docket metadata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resourcing agencies and leveraging public-private partnerships for safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must be given authority and resources to implement technical and procedural reforms; where budget shortfalls exist, civic-minded private-sector actors should partner with government to implement detection and mitigation tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps include funding for IT upgrades, contracting third-party bot detection services, and cooperating with private partners to deploy CAPTCHA, rate limiting, and analytics without unduly burdening public participation.
